title: Scope
subtitle: Lexical environments, scope chain, var vs let/const

cards.front: Lexical vs dynamic scope in JS?
cards.meaning: JavaScript uses lexical (static) scope for variables: which outer bindings a function sees is fixed by where it was written, not by who called it. Dynamic scope would resolve free variables from the caller’s environment; JS does not do that for variables.

cards.front: inner() defined at top level, called from outer() — which x does inner log?
cards.meaning: The x from where inner was defined (e.g. global), not outer’s local x. Call site does not change the lexical scope chain.
cards.example: const x = 1; function outer() { const x = 2; inner(); } function inner() { console.log(x); } // logs 1

cards.front: inner() defined inside outer() — which x does inner log?
cards.meaning: outer’s x (e.g. 2). Because inner is nested in outer’s source, outer’s lexical environment is on inner’s scope chain.
cards.example: const x = 1; function outer() { const x = 2; function inner() { console.log(x); } inner(); } // logs 2

cards.front: Is this the same mechanism as lexical variable scope?
cards.meaning: No. Variables use lexical scope. this is mostly call-site determined — a different mechanism. Do not explain this as “dynamic scope for variables.”

cards.front: Global vs function vs block scope — what creates each?
cards.meaning: Global/module: script or module top level (top-level var/function in scripts; let/const/class; imports in modules). Function: entering a function — parameters, var, and function declarations live there even if written inside nested blocks. Block: a { } (if/for/while/switch/bare); let, const, and class bind to the nearest block.

var is function-scoped (or global at top level) and ignores { }; let/const are block-scoped to the nearest { }. var x = 1; var x = 2; is allowed; redeclaring let/const in the same scope is SyntaxError. Nested let with the same name is shadowing, not redeclaration.
cards.example:
if (true) { var a = 1; let b = 2; } console.log(a); // 1 — console.log(b) ReferenceError
var x = 1; { var x = 2; } console.log(x); // 2

cards.front: var a inside if (flag) — log a after the if when flag is false?
cards.meaning: undefined, not ReferenceError. var is hoisted to the function, so the binding exists even if the assignment never ran. let b in that block never left the block — logging b is ReferenceError.
cards.example: function example(flag) { if (flag) { var a = 1; let b = 2; } console.log(a); }

cards.meaning: None for scope: both are block-scoped the same way. Difference is reassignment: a const binding cannot be reassigned; object/array contents can still mutate.

cards.front: Why does for (let i = ...) fix the setTimeout loop bug?
cards.meaning: for (let i = ...) creates a new i binding per iteration. Each closure closes over a different binding. var gives one function-scoped i shared by every callback, which is the 3, 3, 3 bug (closures unit).
The engine-level backing of a scope: an EnvironmentRecord mapping identifier → binding, plus an outer link to the parent lexical environment (or null). That outer chain is the scope chain.

Start in the current lexical environment; if the name is missing, follow the outer link and repeat until global/module or ReferenceError. Inner does not copy outer values — it walks the chain when the identifier is evaluated. Assignment to a resolved binding updates that binding.

An inner scope declares the same name as an outer scope. Lookup stops at the nearest binding; the outer variable still exists and is visible again after the inner scope ends. Parameters shadow the same way. Redeclaring let in the same scope is SyntaxError, not shadowing.
cards.example:
const x = 'outer'; function f() { const x = 'inner'; console.log(x); } // 'inner'
f(); console.log(x); // 'outer'

cards.meaning: Yes — a block-like environment that holds the err binding. The catch parameter shadows only inside the catch block and does not leak past it.

cards.front: Classic script vs ES module top-level scope?
cards.meaning: Classic scripts share a global environment; default sloppy unless "use strict"; top-level this is the global object. ES modules get their own module scope, are always strict, and top-level this is undefined. Two modules do not share top-level let bindings.
The standard way to refer to the global object across environments. Browser historically window; Node historically global; workers self. Prefer globalThis in portable code.

cards.front: Does every global binding appear on globalThis?
cards.meaning: No. Classic script: top-level var/function become globalThis properties; top-level let/const/class are global bindings but not global-object properties. Module bindings are not global at all — const API_URL in a module is not on window.
cards.example: var fromVar = 1; let fromLet = 2; // classic script: globalThis.fromVar === 1; globalThis.fromLet === undefined

cards.meaning: Sloppy mode: creates an implicit global (a property on the global object). Strict mode, including ES modules: ReferenceError. Prefer const/let and modules.
cards.example: function leak() { leaked = 42; } leak(); globalThis.leaked // 42 sloppy; ReferenceError if 'use strict'
